answers.working:
The last known element, oganesson (\(Z = 118\)), is a noble gas that completes period 7 with the configuration \([\mathrm{Rn}]\,5f^{14}6d^{10}7s^27p^6\).

The next electrons go into a new shell, the 8s orbital. Element 119 would be \([\mathrm{Og}]\,8s^1\) (an alkali metal, group 1) and element 120 would be \([\mathrm{Og}]\,8s^2\), with two electrons in the outermost s orbital, just like Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba and Ra.

So it would belong to group 2, the **alkaline earth metals**. So the answer is option (A).

answers.value: These are isoelectronic and have identical bond order.
answers.working:
Count the electrons in each species:

- \(\mathrm{N_2}\): \(7 + 7 = 14\)
- CO: \(6 + 8 = 14\)
- \(\mathrm{NO^+}\): \(7 + 8 - 1 = 14\)

All three have 14 electrons, so they are **isoelectronic**.

With 14 electrons, the molecular orbital configuration is \(\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^* 1s^2\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^* 2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^2\,\pi 2p_y^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2\). That gives 10 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons, so the bond order is \(\frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3\) for every one of them (a triple bond, \(\mathrm{N{\equiv}N}\), \(\mathrm{C{\equiv}O}\), \(\mathrm{N{\equiv}O^+}\)).

So they are isoelectronic and have the same bond order. So the answer is option (C).

Use the spin-only formula \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. A moment close to 2 BM means \(n = 1\) (\(\sqrt{3} = 1.73\) BM).

| Complex | Metal ion | Ligand field | Unpaired e | \(\mu\) (BM) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) | \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), \(3d^6\) | weak (high spin) | 4 | 4.90 |
| \(\mathrm{[MnCl_4]^{2-}}\) | \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), \(3d^5\) | weak, tetrahedral | 5 | 5.92 |
| \(\mathrm{[Mn(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) | \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), \(3d^5\) | strong \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) (low spin, \(t_{2g}^5\)) | 1 | 1.73 |
| \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) | Ni(0), \(3d^{10}\) | strong CO | 0 | 0 |

Only the cyanide complex of Mn(II) is low spin with one unpaired electron, giving about 1.73 BM, which is close to 2 BM. So the answer is option (D).

answers.label: B
answers.working:
**\(\mathrm{XeF_4}\):** Xe has 8 valence electrons. Four are used in bonds to F, leaving 2 lone pairs. That is 6 electron pairs (octahedral arrangement). The two lone pairs sit opposite each other (trans) to keep apart, so the four F atoms lie in one plane: **square planar**.

**\(\mathrm{SF_4}\):** S has 6 valence electrons. Four bond to F, leaving 1 lone pair. That is 5 electron pairs (trigonal bipyramidal arrangement). The lone pair takes an equatorial position, where it has fewer \(90^\circ\) repulsions, and the shape becomes **see-saw**.

So the shapes are square planar and see-saw, in that order. So the answer is option (B).

answers.label: B
answers.working:
The colour we see is the **complementary colour** of the light the complex absorbs. The stronger the ligand field, the larger the splitting \(\Delta_o\) and the shorter the wavelength absorbed.

In the series given, the ligand field strength rises \(\mathrm{Cl^-} < \mathrm{H_2O} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{CN^-}\):

| Complex | Light absorbed | Colour seen |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{[CoCl(NH_3)_5]^{2+}}\) | about 535 nm, yellow | violet |
| \(\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)(NH_3)_5]^{3+}}\) | about 500 nm, blue-green | red |
| \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) | about 475 nm, blue | yellow-orange |
| \(\mathrm{[Co(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) | about 310 nm, ultraviolet | pale yellow |

The complex with the weakest field (one \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\)) absorbs the longest wavelength, yellow light, and so appears violet. So the answer is option (B).

answers.working:
Both drawings are the same molecule, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2F}\) (1-fluoropropan-2-ol): the front carbon carries H, \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) and OH, and the back carbon carries F, H and H. So they cannot be structural or positional isomers.

The front carbon is a stereocentre, so we must check whether the two drawings have the same configuration. Read its three groups going clockwise around the front carbon:

- Left drawing: H (left) then \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) (right) then OH (down).
- Right drawing: OH (left) then H (right) then \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) (down), which is the same cyclic order H, \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), OH.

The same cyclic order with the back carbon in the same place means the same configuration (both are S). The right drawing is just the left one with the front carbon turned by \(120^\circ\) about the C-C bond and the back \(\mathrm{CH_2F}\) group rotated too. Rotation about a single bond gives **conformations**, not enantiomers.

So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: D
answers.working:
Electron-withdrawing nitro groups at the ortho and para positions stabilise the phenoxide ion by resonance, so they increase the acidity of a phenol.

- **P**, picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol), has three nitro groups and is a very strong acid, \(\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 0.4\).
- **N**, benzoic acid, \(\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 4.2\): a carboxylic acid is far more acidic than ordinary phenols.
- **Q**, 4-nitrophenol, \(\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 7.1\): one nitro group helps, but not enough to beat a carboxylic acid.
- **M**, phenol, \(\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 10\).

A lower \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) means a stronger acid, so the order is \(\mathbf{P} > \mathbf{N} > \mathbf{Q} > \mathbf{M}\). The tempting option (A) puts benzoic acid above picric acid, but three nitro groups make picric acid stronger than benzoic acid. So the answer is option (D).

answers.label: C
answers.working:
**First sequence.** Hypophosphorous acid reduces a diazonium salt, replacing \(\mathrm{N_2^+}\) by H: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + H_3PO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_6 + N_2 + H_3PO_3 + HCl}\). So M is benzene.

Benzene with CO and HCl in the presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) is the **Gattermann-Koch reaction**, which puts a CHO group on the ring. So N is benzaldehyde, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\).

**Second sequence.** \(\mathrm{SnCl_2}\) and HCl reduce a nitrile to an imine (**Stephen reaction**): P is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH{=}NH}\). Acid hydrolysis of the imine gives the aldehyde, so Q is also \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\).

Both N and Q are benzaldehyde. So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: C
answers.working:
Work backwards from the product, benzalacetone \(\mathrm{PhCH{=}CHCOCH_3}\). It is formed by a **cross aldol (Claisen-Schmidt) condensation** in dilute NaOH: \(\mathrm{PhCHO + CH_3COCH_3 \rightarrow PhCH{=}CHCOCH_3 + H_2O}\). Benzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen and acts only as the carbonyl partner, while acetone supplies the carbanion. So Y is acetone and Z is benzaldehyde.

Y comes from an alkyne by hydration with \(\mathrm{HgSO_4}\) and dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) (Markovnikov addition, then the enol turns into a ketone). Propyne gives acetone: \(\mathrm{CH_3C{\equiv}CH + H_2O \rightarrow CH_3COCH_3}\). So X is propyne.

But-2-yne (option D) would give butanone, which would put an extra carbon in the product, and the phenyl alkynes in (A) and (B) would put the phenyl group on the ketone side. So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: D
answers.working:
**M** has a six-membered ring (five C and one O), so it is a **pyranose**. The \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) on C5 points up, which marks a D-sugar, and the OH groups on C2, C3 and C4 (down, up, down) match glucose. At the anomeric carbon C1 (the carbon next to the ring O on the right), the OH points down, on the opposite side to the \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\). That is the **\(\alpha\)** anomer. So M is \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucopyranose.

**N** has a five-membered ring (four C and one O), so it is a **furanose**. The anomeric carbon C2 carries both an OH and a \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) (C1), as fructose does. C5 has its \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) up (D-sugar), and the anomeric OH on C2 is also up, on the same side as that \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\). That is the **\(\beta\)** anomer. So N is \(\beta\)-D-(\(-\))-fructofuranose.

These are the two units that join to make sucrose. So the answer is option (D).

answers.working:
Use \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\); the reaction is spontaneous when \(\Delta G < 0\).

- The reaction is exothermic, so \(\Delta H < 0\).
- A solid turns into a solid plus two gases, so the disorder increases a lot: \(\Delta S > 0\).

Then \(\Delta H\) is negative and \(-T\Delta S\) is also negative at every temperature, so \(\Delta G\) is always negative.

The reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures. So the answer is option (D).

**Work function** (from the threshold wavelength 500 nm):

\(W_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{500 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.96 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**Energy of one 300 nm photon:**

\(E = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{300 \times 10^{-9}} = 6.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Kinetic energy of each photoelectron: \(6.6 \times 10^{-19} - 3.96 \times 10^{-19} = 2.64 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\).

**Photons per second** from a 100 W bulb: \(\dfrac{100}{6.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.515 \times 10^{20}\). Taking one electron per photon, this many electrons are ejected each second.

Total kinetic energy per second \(= 1.515 \times 10^{20} \times 2.64 \times 10^{-19} = 40\ \mathrm{J}\). (Quick check: the fraction of each photon's energy left as kinetic energy is \(1 - \frac{300}{500} = 0.4\), and \(0.4 \times 100 = 40\).)

Option (C), \(2.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J, is the energy of just one electron. So the answer is option (A).

answers.value: Plot of [R] against t: a straight line falling from near the top of the [R] axis
answers.working:
The units of the rate constant tell us the order. For an nth-order reaction, k has units \(\mathrm{(mol\ L^{-1})^{1-n}\ s^{-1}}\). Here k is in \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), so \(1 - n = 1\) and \(n = 0\): a **zero-order** reaction.

For a zero-order reaction, \([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\). A plot of [R] against t is a straight line with intercept \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) and slope \(-k\), falling steadily.

The other plots (a straight falling line of \(\ln[\mathrm{R}]\), a straight rising line of \(\log\frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\), and an exponential decay of [R]) all describe a **first-order** reaction, whose k would be in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

So the answer is option (B).

answers.value: Plot of \(\Pi\) against V from (0,0): a curve falling very steeply close to the \(\Pi\) axis, then flattening just above the V axis
answers.working:
Osmotic pressure is \(\Pi = CRT = \dfrac{n}{V}RT\). For a fixed amount of solute (n fixed) at a fixed temperature, \(nRT\) is a constant, so \(\Pi V = \text{constant}\), that is \(\Pi \propto \dfrac{1}{V}\).

The graph of \(\Pi\) against V is therefore a **rectangular hyperbola**: as V becomes very small, \(\Pi\) rises without limit (the curve hugs the \(\Pi\) axis but never meets it), and as V becomes large, \(\Pi\) falls towards zero (the curve approaches the V axis).

Option (B) is also a falling curve, but it starts at a finite value on the \(\Pi\) axis, which would mean a finite pressure at zero volume; that is the shape of an exponential decay, not \(1/V\). The straight lines in (C) and (D) do not fit an inverse relation. So the answer is option (A).

KCl is a strong electrolyte, so it follows the **Kohlrausch (Debye-Huckel-Onsager) equation**: \(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}\).

The square roots of the two concentrations are \(\sqrt{1 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.01\) and \(\sqrt{9 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.03\). So:

\(149.1 = \Lambda_m^\circ - 0.01A\)

\(147.1 = \Lambda_m^\circ - 0.03A\)

Subtracting: \(2.0 = 0.02A\), so \(A = 100\). Then \(\Lambda_m^\circ = 149.1 + 0.01 \times 100 = 150.1\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).

So the answer is option (B).
